title: Augustus Exiles His Daughter Julia
text:
Julia was the only child of the emperor Augustus. He used her as a tool of dynastic policy. At fourteen she was married to her cousin Marcellus, who died two years later. Then she was married to Agrippa, Augustus's closest general, a man a generation older, and bore him five children. When Agrippa died, Augustus made his stepson Tiberius divorce a wife he loved in order to marry Julia. The marriage was unhappy, and Tiberius withdrew to Rhodes.

In 2 BC Augustus learned, or was persuaded, that his daughter had taken lovers among the young nobles of Rome, among them a son of Mark Antony. According to Suetonius, he sent an account of the matter to the senate in writing, being too ashamed to appear, and banished her to the tiny island of Pandateria. Her mother, Scribonia, whom Augustus had divorced on the day Julia was born, chose to go into exile with her.

Suetonius says that Augustus forbade Julia wine and every comfort, and allowed no man to visit her without his permission, after a detailed description of the visitor's appearance. When the people of Rome begged him to bring her back, he refused. He used to quote a line of Homer, wishing he had never married and had died without children, and called Julia, his granddaughter and his grandson his three running sores. Even in his will he forbade that she be buried in his tomb.
lesson: Children used as instruments of ambition may never find a way home. A parent who treats a child as a policy loses the child.
people: Augustus, Julia the Elder, Scribonia, Tiberius
source: Suetonius, Life of Augustus 63 to 65 and 101; Cassius Dio, Roman History 55.10
caveat: Some historians think the adultery charges covered a political conspiracy.
